f: Calum Scott carried a persistent voice in the back of his mind telling him it was only a matter of time before his success disappeared—a feeling amplified by being "a lad from Hull" in an industry where he often felt he didn't belong. Writing his third album 'Avanoir' silenced that doubt, allowing him to reach a new level of confidence and creative freedom he had never experienced before.

For much of his career, Scott battled the classic imposter syndrome narrative: despite his achievements and recognition, he couldn't shake the feeling that he wasn't truly worthy of what he'd accomplished. As discussed in Hull Trains – Moving Minds , this inner voice intensified with the spotlight on him, creating a cycle of self-doubt that many high-achievers recognize.

What changed was the realisation that he was genuinely here to stay. By the time he began working on his third album, Scott made a conscious shift: he stopped accepting the narrative that his career was temporary or fragile. This mindset breakthrough opened the door to a completely different creative process.
From self-doubt to creative freedom with 'Avanoir'

The album 'Avanoir', released in October, became a turning point. Scott didn't just record songs; he reclaimed his artistic identity. In the podcast episode , he reflects that with this album he "just feel[s] more confident and more content than I ever have."

This confidence translated into a broader creative range. Instead of limiting himself to what he thought the audience wanted—emotional, tear-inducing ballads—he felt free to explore different styles and themes. The album allowed him to write what he genuinely wanted, not just what he believed would be commercially successful or emotionally manipulative.

From resistance to mental resilience

When Scott first encountered these mirror exercises in therapy, he felt initially uncomfortable with the practice , describing it as feeling "stupid." But he committed to the process anyway, recognizing a fundamental truth about how the mind works through repetition.

The turning point came when he realized that positive affirmations operate on the same neural principle as negative self-talk —when you hear something enough times, whether it's harmful or healing, your brain internalizes it as truth. For Scott, this wasn't abstract psychology; it was a practical path out of the self-criticism and imposter syndrome that had shadowed his career for years.
As Scott explains in the episode , therapy wasn't just about talking through problems—it was about installing new mental habits through consistent, deliberate practice.

"Therapy, hands down, saved my life. Debs, my mum Debs, definitely was the core anchor as to why I'm still here. But therapy helped me reinforce all of that strength and helped me build a strong and unwavering support mentally."

The confidence came from small, repeated wins rather than a single dramatic break.
Staying grounded while climbing

One of the most telling details of Marriner-Brown's transition is that he didn't completely abandon his previous work. He maintained freelance gardening clients in Bridlington and occasionally helped with his parents' flower business—deliberate choices that kept him anchored to something tangible while navigating the uncertainty of a new career path.

This dual commitment served a psychological purpose too. Early failure in reality television can trigger imposter syndrome and anxiety, especially when stepping into a professional environment as a newcomer. For Marriner-Brown, getting outdoors and working with his hands helped him manage those feelings during the volatile early months of his broadcasting career.

bc12ac5697.q: How does brain injury impact memory and cognitive function during recovery, and what support strategies can help compensate for these deficits?
bc12ac5697.a: After brain injury, working memory becomes really poor. Jobs that would have taken five minutes took half an hour, and Paul found himself forgetting tools, policies and procedures. He emphasizes that the brain is complex and individual—unlike a broken arm with a clear treatment plan, brain injury survivors receive few answers. Over time, Paul learned coping strategies such as using lists, reminders, and setting himself up to win, though he notes not everyone has access to a neuropsychologist to guide them.

b97d9d39eb.q: What are the hidden challenges of brain injury beyond physical symptoms, particularly in social and professional contexts?
b97d9d39eb.a: Brain injury survivors often look okay on the surface when walking and talking, which leads others to misunderstand their struggles. Paul could not articulate how he was feeling and had poor insight into how his brain was different. He was unable to leave the house alone for the first four months after brain injury and had to be chaperoned by family and friends. People would misinterpret his behavior as awkward or confrontational because he lacked the speed of thought to explain his condition, making him extremely vulnerable in the world.
f: Brain injury survivors often look physically fine while walking and talking, yet face profound invisible struggles that others misinterpret . They may lack the speed of thought to explain their condition, poor insight into their own cognitive changes, and extreme vulnerability in social and professional settings—challenges that extend far beyond what a broken arm or visible injury would reveal.

When Paul Spence suffered a frontal lobe brain hemorrhage in 2012, the physical recovery was just the beginning. For the first four months after his injury, he was unable to leave the house alone and required constant supervision from family and friends. Yet from the outside, he appeared unharmed—a fact that proved deeply isolating and misunderstood.

The cruelest aspect of brain injury is that it remains invisible. Paul could not articulate how he was feeling or communicate the depth of his cognitive changes. Because he maintained his physical ability to walk and speak, people in his world assumed he was recovering normally. When his behavior seemed awkward or confrontational, others attributed it to personality rather than recognizing it as a symptom of his injury. Paul shares the specifics of these behavioral changes and how they affected his relationships in the full episode.

The lack of speed in cognitive processing compounded this isolation. Brain injury doesn't just slow thinking—it can make it nearly impossible to articulate internal struggles in real time. People would misinterpret his slower responses as rudeness or conflict-avoidance , when in reality he was fighting to process information and formulate responses. This gap between internal reality and external perception left him extremely vulnerable in the world.
"I am different, I am no less—I've been judging myself as a less of a person, and it was not fair. I needed encouragement, kindness and compassion."

Paul Spence — CEO and Founder of P.A.U.L For Brain Recovery. An electrical engineer who survived a frontal lobe brain hemorrhage in 2012, Paul spent two years in neuropsychology treatment after losing his job due to lasting cognitive deficits. He transformed his recovery journey through structured exercise and fundraising, launching a Facebook page that sparked community demand and ultimately led to founding P.A.U.L For Brain Recovery, now an NHS-commissioned service dedicated to supporting brain injury survivors through comprehensive rehabilitation.

8641ed4873.q: What role did structured exercise and goal-setting play in recovery from brain injury?
8641ed4873.a: Paul started with a small home workout of five press-ups, five sit-ups, and five squats, which gave his family hope and provided structure to his day and week. He then progressed to running, starting with a run-walk around the block, then running a mile. On the anniversary of his injury, he organized a half marathon with 70 friends and family members, raising £17,000 for Hull Royal Infirmary. The goal-setting and structure of training for these events provided accountability and positive focus during his negative recovery period.
f: Exercise and goal-setting transformed Paul Spence's brain injury recovery by providing daily structure, accountability, and a concrete path forward during an otherwise uncertain period. Starting with just five press-ups, five sit-ups, and five squats at home, he progressed to running, eventually organizing a half marathon that raised £17,000 for Hull Royal Infirmary—turning physical rehabilitation into a meaningful mission that gave his family and community tangible hope.
From Five Press-Ups to a Half Marathon: The Power of Incremental Progress

The recovery process began with simplicity. Paul's first home workout—five press-ups, five sit-ups, and five squats—was deliberately modest, but its impact was profound. This small structured routine gave his family hope that recovery was possible and provided his day and week with rhythmic purpose. When you are told you may never be the same again and face months of uncertainty, even a five-exercise routine becomes a psychological anchor.

From there, the progression followed a clear trajectory: run-walk around the block, then a full mile, then longer distances. Each milestone built on the last, creating what Paul Spence discusses in the episode as a series of achievable targets. This wasn't random fitness; it was purposeful rehabilitation with visible endpoints.
From Personal Recovery to Community Mission

The turning point came on the anniversary of his brain hemorrhage, when Paul organized a half marathon with 70 friends and family members. The event raised £17,000 for Hull Royal Infirmary —the hospital that had saved his life. This single event crystallized the psychological shift: his recovery was no longer just about him. It was about giving back, creating meaning, and transforming his struggle into a collective act of gratitude and support.

5fd140fc20.q: How does therapeutic intervention and mental health support contribute to brain injury recovery and identity reconstruction?
5fd140fc20.a: After two years of recovery, Paul accessed mental health services and saw a psychotherapist who helped him reframe his thinking. A critical breakthrough was his psychotherapist telling him 'I am different, I am no less'—he realized he had been judging himself as a lesser person rather than simply a changed person. Through therapy, he cultivated positive self-talk and became his own best friend rather than his own harshest critic, which supported both his psychological recovery and his healthy lifestyle choices.
f: After two years of recovery, accessing psychotherapy became the turning point: a psychotherapist helped Paul Spence reframe his relationship with his changed identity through a critical insight— "I am different, I am no less." Through therapy, he shifted from judging himself as a lesser person to recognizing himself as simply changed, and cultivated positive self-talk that became essential to both psychological recovery and sustained lifestyle choices.

The power of this reframing cannot be overstated. Brain injury survivors often internalize a narrative of diminishment, comparing their present selves to their pre-injury capabilities. Paul's breakthrough came not from denying the changes—his cognitive deficits, his altered abilities, his lost job as an electrical engineer—but from accepting change while refusing self-judgment. The psychotherapist did not minimize his struggles; instead, she offered him a more compassionate framework for understanding them.
"I am different, I am no less—I've been judging myself as a less of a person, and it was not fair. I needed encouragement, kindness and compassion."

Paul Spence — CEO and Founder of P.A.U.L For Brain Recovery, Lecturer at University of Hull. After suffering a frontal lobe brain hemorrhage in 2012 following an unprovoked attack, Spence spent time in the major trauma ward at Hull Royal Infirmary ICU. Following two years of neuropsychology treatment and recovery, he lost his job due to lasting cognitive deficits. He transformed his recovery through structured exercise and fundraising efforts, eventually founding P.A.U.L For Brain Recovery, now an NHS-commissioned service supporting other survivors through their own recovery journeys.

This shift from self-criticism to self-compassion is not merely psychological comfort—it has tangible effects on recovery outcomes. Positive self-talk directly supported both his mental health and his physical lifestyle choices, creating a feedback loop where psychological improvement enabled better decisions about exercise, routine, and engagement. When Paul began viewing himself as his own best friend rather than his harshest critic, the motivation to care for himself fundamentally changed.

The therapeutic work was not about erasing loss or pretending the injury hadn't happened. As detailed in this episode of Hull Trains – Moving Minds , Paul continued to experience real cognitive challenges—working memory deficits, tasks that took three times longer than before, professional capabilities that had permanently shifted. What changed was his emotional relationship to those facts. Therapy provided the cognitive tools to separate the injury's impact from his worth as a person.

a55485d8e5.q: What inspired the founding of a brain injury recovery charity, and how did community relationships drive its creation?
a55485d8e5.a: After running marathons and organizing fundraising events, Paul launched a Facebook page to give insight into brain injury and serve as a voice for others. People began messaging him asking him to visit their family members, and he started going out in the community sitting with people in recovery. He found that people would say 'you get it' because they felt he understood their lived experience—something no statistic or neuroscience report could replace. This community demand made him realize there was a need for accessible support, leading him to seek a business plan and formal charity registration.

bc279affe8.q: What role did mentorship and networking play in transforming a personal recovery story into an established NHS-commissioned charity?
bc279affe8.a: Paul met local businessman Neil Hudgel at a networking event and was invited to be an ambassador for Hudgel Solicitors. Neil was instrumental in developing P.A.U.L For Brain Recovery, helping with the business plan and opening doors for the charity. Neil introduced Paul to Emma Latimer, the NHS chief officer, creating access to the healthcare system. Paul notes that while Neil never held his hand, he opened doors and encouraged Paul to step out of his comfort zone, demonstrating that 'it's not what you know, it's who you know at times,' and reinforcing the importance of never undervaluing yourself and always showing up.

3cceb9b598.q: How has P.A.U.L For Brain Recovery evolved from a personal initiative into a structured organization with partnerships and staff?
3cceb9b598.a: The charity was commissioned by the NHS in 2017, which enabled Paul to develop a team. He brought on Lee North as operations manager 10 years ago to handle policies, procedures, governance, insurance and all the administrative work—areas Paul, as an electrician, had no previous knowledge of. The organization now has a team of eight staff members, soon to be 10, plus volunteers, ambassadors, and trustees. Paul has also developed partnerships with the University of Hull, working with five different departments and collaborating with researchers like Dr. Kelly Doherty and Professor Jonathan Glashard on a brain health board.
f: The NHS commission in 2017 was the turning point that transformed Paul Spence's personal recovery journey into a legitimate, staffed organization. He brought on Lee North as operations manager to handle governance, policies, and administration—areas Paul, as an electrician, had no expertise in. Today, the charity operates with eight staff members, soon to be ten, alongside volunteers, ambassadors, and trustees, plus formal partnerships with five departments at the University of Hull.
From Solo Mission to Structured Team

Paul Spence began as a sole voice—an electrical engineer sharing his brain injury recovery story through fundraising events and social media. The transformation accelerated significantly when the NHS commissioned P.A.U.L For Brain Recovery in 2017 . This endorsement gave him the credibility and resources needed to move beyond a grassroots initiative.

The first major structural decision was recruiting Lee North as operations manager. North's appointment ten years ago filled a critical gap —handling policies, procedures, governance, insurance, and administrative compliance that would have been beyond Paul's background as an engineer. This hire allowed Spence to focus on the mission while someone else managed the organizational machinery.
Building Academic Credibility and Research Partnerships

Beyond staffing, Spence developed formal partnerships that anchored the charity in academic rigor. The organization now collaborates with five different departments at the University of Hull , working alongside researchers like Dr. Kelly Doherty and Professor Jonathan Glashard on a brain health board. These partnerships lend research credibility to the charity's work and open pathways for evidence-based practice.

Social media will always contain both praise and criticism, but neither determines your value or performance. The strategy is straightforward: live in the present, improve each day, and represent your club and yourself with integrity; external commentary is something to acknowledge but not absorb.
The Practice of Selective Mental Filtering

Jack Charles advises treating social media as background noise rather than instruction. He recognizes that negative comments are inevitable during a club transition , especially when moving between rival organizations, but dwelling on them serves no practical purpose.

His approach centers on a single principle: separate what lies within your control from what does not. Training quality, mental resilience, team representation, and personal conduct—these are controllable. Social media sentiment, opponent criticism, and public opinion—these are not. As discussed in the episode, Jack emphasizes that external pressure becomes manageable once you stop treating it as your responsibility to manage .
Protecting Family from the Noise

Charles extends this mindset to those around him, particularly advising family members to actively avoid reading negative comments online. Protecting emotional space—both personal and familial—is part of the discipline . When family members absorb negativity on behalf of the player, it creates secondary stress that can undermine focus.

f: Family presence during crisis becomes the foundation of survival itself . When Gemma faced a heart attack while raising her young son, her brother Chris never turned his back—and that unconditional presence through the darkest period became the turning point in both her physical recovery and mental health healing.

The difference between surviving a health crisis and actually recovering from it often hinges on one simple factor: who stays when things fall apart . Gemma credits her brother Chris with her survival, describing a period when she was seriously ill—including a heart attack that occurred around her son's birth—and the weight she was carrying felt unbearable. In that darkness, Chris did not disappear.

This is not about grand gestures or perfect words. It is about presence itself. As Chris explains in the episode , family support works because "we're all family, we all look after each other as best we can and be there to support each other." The philosophy is simple, but its power is profound.
Presence over Perfection — How Showing Up Transforms Recovery

When someone is drowning in both physical illness and mental health struggles, they don't need rescuers with all the answers. They need someone who will sit with them in the difficulty without abandoning ship. Gemma's experience reveals that showing up consistently, even during the hardest months, becomes the anchor that prevents further descent into crisis.

Chris's willingness to be present during Gemma's period of serious illness—when she was vulnerable, unwell, and managing mental health challenges alongside cardiac trauma—created safety. Safety is the soil in which recovery begins. A point detailed in this podcast , Chris himself later faced his own mental health struggles during his captaincy at Hull Kingston Rovers, experiences he kept private at a time when the sport did not openly discuss such challenges. Yet the family structure of unconditional support remained intact.
